html:
Dënéndeh, "the land of the people", is the homeland of the Dene, the Athabaskan peoples of the boreal forest and tundra of northwestern Canada. On the map it is a huge shape across the Northwest Territories and the north of the western provinces.

The Dene include the Denesuline (Chipewyan), Tłı̨chǫ (Dogrib), Dehcho (Slavey), Sahtu and Gwich'in, among others. In 1492 they lived in small family bands, hunting caribou and moose, snaring hare, fishing the great lakes and rivers, and travelling by canoe in summer and snowshoe and toboggan in winter.

From the late 1700s the Hudson's Bay Company and the North West Company set up fur posts along the Mackenzie River, and missionaries followed. After oil and gold finds, Canada signed Treaty 8 in 1899 and Treaty 11 in 1921 with Dene leaders, who later said they had agreed to peace, not to giving up land. In 1975 the Dene Declaration asserted their right to govern themselves, and the Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Inquiry of the 1970s backed a delay of the gas pipeline. Regional land claims followed, including those of the Gwich'in and the Sahtu.
